lesson.title: Endosymbiotic Theory: How One Cell Swallowing Another Changed Life Forever
lesson.summary: Endosymbiotic theory holds that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell and became permanent, essential residents inside it.
lesson.body:
You have already studied prokaryotic cells, which lack a nucleus and internal membrane bound organelles, as well as mitochondria and chloroplasts, the organelles inside eukaryotic cells responsible for cellular respiration and photosynthesis respectively. Endosymbiotic theory connects these two topics with a striking claim: mitochondria and chloroplasts are not organelles that eukaryotic cells built from scratch. They are the descendants of once free-living prokaryotic organisms that were engulfed by a larger host cell and, over time, became permanent internal partners rather than separate organisms. The biologist most associated with developing and championing this idea, in the face of considerable early skepticism, is Lynn Margulis, working primarily in the 1960s and 1970s.

The evidence supporting this theory is unusually strong and comes from several independent directions, which is exactly what makes it convincing rather than merely a clever story. First, mitochondria and chloroplasts each contain their own small, circular DNA molecule, structurally similar to a prokaryotic chromosome rather than the linear, histone wrapped chromosomes found in the eukaryotic nucleus. Second, both organelles are surrounded by a double membrane: an inner membrane thought to derive from the original prokaryote's own cell membrane, and an outer membrane thought to derive from the host cell's membrane that formed around it during engulfment. Third, both organelles are roughly bacteria sized and reproduce by a process resembling bacterial binary fission, dividing on their own timeline somewhat independently of the host cell's own division cycle. Fourth, their ribosomes are structurally more similar to bacterial ribosomes than to the ribosomes found elsewhere in the eukaryotic cytoplasm.

This is where molecular evidence for evolution becomes especially powerful. When biologists compare the DNA sequences found in mitochondria to sequences from various groups of bacteria, mitochondrial DNA consistently shows the closest similarity to a group called alpha-proteobacteria, a group that includes some free-living aerobic bacteria efficient at using oxygen to generate energy. Chloroplast DNA, by the same kind of comparison, shows closest similarity to cyanobacteria, a group of photosynthetic bacteria. These sequence comparisons point specifically to which ancestral groups were likely engulfed, not just that engulfment happened in general.

The two organelles are thought to have arisen at different times: mitochondria first, from the engulfment of an aerobic, alpha-proteobacterium-like ancestor, and chloroplasts later, from a separate engulfment of a cyanobacterium-like ancestor, in the lineage that eventually gave rise to plants and algae. Many of the exact details, such as whether the initial relationship began as predation, parasitism, or something else, and the precise sequence and timing of events, are still actively researched and debated. What is not seriously disputed among biologists today is the core claim itself: once a fairly radical proposal, endosymbiotic theory is now a well supported and broadly accepted part of how biologists explain the origin of these two organelles.
